list.name: deployment_environment
list.label: Environment
list.description: Sourced from the metric, not target_info. The OTel Java agent here emits the pre-semconv-1.27 attribute deployment.environment -> label deployment_environment. target_info additionally exposes deployment_environment_name, which does NOT exist on the metric series - reading the variable from target_info produced a value that matched nothing.

list.name: service_name
list.label: Service
list.description: Sourced from the application metric, NOT from target_info. Prometheus' OTLP receiver turns service.name into the `job` label and strips it from target_info (keep_identifying_resource_attributes only exists in Prometheus 3.2+), so label_values(target_info, service_name) returns nothing on 2.55. promote_resource_attributes does put service_name on the metrics themselves, which is what this queries.

list.name: log_level
list.label: Log level
list.description: Loki 3.x derives detected_level automatically. Set to '.+' to see every line regardless of level.
list.query: error and warn : error|warn,errors only : error,all levels : .+

list.name: traceID
list.label: Selected Trace ID
list.description: Populated automatically when you click a row in the API REQUESTS table. You can also paste a trace ID here.

list.name: status_min
list.label: Trace min HTTP status
list.description: TraceQL numeric floor on span.http.response.status_code. Display text vs substituted value: 'All' -> 0.

options.content:
**Prometheus** = *how is the system performing?*  •  **Tempo** = *why was this one request slow?*  •  **Loki** = *what was logged?*  •  **Kubernetes** = *is the infrastructure healthy?*

Flow: pick **Environment → Namespace → Service** → read **Golden Signals** → find the endpoint in **API Endpoint Performance** → click it to filter → pick a request in **API Requests** → click its **Trace ID** and the waterfall plus its logs load below, in this same window.

*This gateway is bursty — measured idle in 64% of five-minute windows. Latency percentiles are undefined while traffic is paused, so those lines bridge idle gaps rather than break. Counters correctly read 0. Judge health over hours, not minutes.*

panels.title: Metrics freshness
panels.description:
Simple: How old the newest metric data is — should normally stay under a minute or two.

Seconds since Prometheus last received an application metric sample over OTLP. Green = pipeline healthy. Red / No data = the collector is no longer delivering metrics to Prometheus, which makes every PromQL panel on this dashboard look empty or stale. Check the TELEMETRY PIPELINE HEALTH row at the bottom.

panels.title: START HERE — METRIC DISCOVERY (open this whenever panels are empty)
Which metric families actually exist in Prometheus (no filters at all)
panels.description:
Simple: Lists every metric Prometheus currently has, ignoring all dashboard filters — confirms data is arriving at all.

Deliberately unfiltered and unscoped, so no dashboard variable can make it lie. If http_server_request_duration_seconds_count is MISSING here, the application's own OTLP metrics are not reaching Prometheus and no dashboard change can help — fix the pipeline. If calls_total / duration_milliseconds_* ARE here, open the SPANMETRICS FALLBACK row below: it rebuilds the golden signals and the endpoint table from the trace stream instead.

panels.title: How stale is each family (seconds since its newest sample)
panels.description:
Simple: How many seconds since each metric type last got new data — green means it's current.

Green means Prometheus is currently being fed that family. Red or absent means the series exists in TSDB but nothing new is arriving — which is exactly what makes instant queries return 'No data' while range queries still show history.

panels.title: SPANMETRICS FALLBACK — RED metrics rebuilt from traces (works while the app's OTLP metrics are down)

options.content:
Your collector runs a **spanmetrics connector** (`05-otel-collector.yaml`) with `http.request.method`, `http.response.status_code` and `http.route` as dimensions. It derives RED metrics from the trace stream, so it keeps working even when the application's own OTLP metrics are being rejected — and your Pipeline Health row shows spans flowing at ~40/s with **zero** failures.

Through the Prometheus OTLP receiver these arrive as `traces_span_metrics_calls_total` and `traces_span_metrics_duration_milliseconds_{bucket,sum,count}` — confirmed present in your Prometheus on 2026-08-11. Note `traces_spanmetrics_calls_total` (no underscore between span and metrics) also exists: that one is Tempo's metrics-generator, which has no `http_route` dimension and cannot back an endpoint table.

Stated plainly: these are **trace-derived and sampling-dependent**, not the authoritative server histogram. Latency here is in **milliseconds**, and the resolution is the 11 explicit buckets from the collector config, so percentiles are coarser than the app's own histogram. This is a working substitute, not a replacement.

panels.title: Request rate by endpoint (spanmetrics)
panels.description: Simple: How many requests per second each endpoint gets, rebuilt from trace data as a backup source.

panels.title: P95 latency by endpoint (spanmetrics)
panels.description: Simple: The slow end of response times per endpoint (95th percentile), rebuilt from trace data as a backup source.

panels.title: Errors by endpoint (spanmetrics)
panels.description:
Simple: Error rate per endpoint, rebuilt from trace data as a backup source.

Per-route series only appear once a route has actually errored. The TOTAL line is pinned with `or vector(0)` so a healthy service shows a flat zero instead of an empty panel.

panels.title: API Endpoint Performance (spanmetrics)
panels.description:
Simple: Same request/latency/error breakdown as the main endpoint table, but sourced from traces instead of the app's own metrics.

Same shape as the Prometheus endpoint table, rebuilt from calls_total / duration_milliseconds_*. Latency columns are milliseconds. Clicking a row sets the same API Route + Method variables, so the Tempo trace drilldown below still works unchanged.

links.title: Drill into this endpoint (sets API Route + Method)

panels.title: Requests (selected range)
panels.description: Simple: Total number of requests in the selected time window.

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Simple: How many requests per second the service is handling right now.

panels.title: Success rate (non-5xx)
panels.description: Simple: Percent of requests that did NOT return a server error.

panels.title: 4xx rate
panels.description: Simple: Percent of requests rejected as bad or unauthorized client requests.

panels.title: 5xx rate
panels.description: Simple: Percent of requests that failed due to a server-side error.

panels.title: Average latency
panels.description:
Simple: The average time it takes to respond to a request.

sum(rate(_sum)) / sum(rate(_count)). NOTE: v9 wrapped the denominator in clamp_min(...,1), which silently divided by 1 whenever RPS < 1 and reported a near-zero average. That clamp is removed here.

panels.title: P95 latency
panels.description: Simple: 95% of requests were faster than this — shows how slow it gets for the slower few.

panels.title: P99 latency
panels.description: Simple: 99% of requests were faster than this — the worst-case tail, excluding the rarest outliers.

panels.title: Traffic by HTTP status class
panels.description: Simple: Request volume over time, broken down by response status code.

panels.title: Latency percentiles (service)
panels.description:
Simple: How response time (P50/P95/P99) has changed over time for the whole service.

Click a purple exemplar diamond to jump straight to the trace that produced that data point.

panels.title: API ENDPOINT PERFORMANCE  —  click a row to drill into that endpoint
API Endpoint Performance
panels.description:
Simple: Every endpoint's request count, speed, and error rate side by side — click a row to drill into just that endpoint.

PROMETHEUS / PromQL. One row per METHOD + ROUTE. All targets are instant queries using increase()/rate() so they follow the time picker. v9 used hardcoded [1h] windows and clamp_min(...,1) denominators; both are fixed here. Click any row: 'Drill into this endpoint' sets the API Route + Method dashboard variables, which drives the SELECTED ENDPOINT row and the Tempo trace list below.

targets.expr: 100 * (sum by (endpoint) (label_join(increase(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[$__range]), "endpoint", " ", "http_request_method", "http_route")) or sum by (endpoint) (label_join(increase(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace"}[$__range]), "endpoint", " ", "http_request_method", "http_route")) * 0) / sum by (endpoint) (label_join(increase(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace"}[$__range]), "endpoint", " ", "http_request_method", "http_route"))

links.title: Drill into this endpoint (sets API Route + Method)
Open this endpoint's traces in Explore (Tempo)

panels.title: Selected endpoint — request rate by status
panels.description: Simple: Request volume for the one endpoint you clicked, broken down by response status.

panels.title: Selected endpoint — latency percentiles
panels.description: Simple: Response time trend (P50/P95/P99) for just the one endpoint you clicked.

panels.title: Selected endpoint — latency distribution (heatmap)
panels.description:
Simple: A heat-map of how response times are distributed for this endpoint — shows whether slowness is a rare outlier or a persistent band.

Renders the raw histogram buckets. Bi-modal bands here mean the endpoint has two distinct code paths (e.g. cache hit vs DB round-trip) — pick a slow request from the trace list below to see which.

panels.title: API REQUESTS — click any row to load its waterfall below
panels.description:
Simple: A list of real individual requests — click one to load its full step-by-step trace below.

TEMPO / TraceQL, tableType = spans. kind=server keeps background jobs (OutboxRelay.relay) out of the list; select() supplies the method / route / status / pod columns.

CLICK THE 'Trace ID' COLUMN — that cell carries the drilldown link. It rewrites the dashboard URL with var-traceID, which the waterfall panel and the Loki panel below both read. Clicking any other column does nothing.

Grafana cannot expand a waterfall inside a table panel; a table row -> data link -> dashboard variable -> traces panel round-trip is the supported pattern. It stays in this browser tab, so it still reads as one window.

targets.query: { resource.service.name = "$service_name" && kind = server && span.http.route =~ "$http_operation" && span.http.request.method =~ "$http_method" && span.http.response.status_code >= $status_min && duration >= $min_duration } | select(span.http.request.method, span.http.route, span.http.response.status_code, resource.k8s.pod.name, resource.service.version)

panels.title: SELECTED TRACE — FULL WATERFALL:  HTTP → Controller → Service → Repository → JDBC → SQL → DB → Downstream
panels.description:
Simple: The exact path one specific request took through the app, step by step, showing where the time was actually spent.

TEMPO / TraceQL trace-by-ID lookup on ${traceID}.

'No data found in response' here means the Selected Trace ID variable is still empty — click the Trace ID column in the API REQUESTS table above, or paste an ID into the box at the top of the dashboard.

Expand spans to read attributes: db.statement, db.system, Hikari pool timings, downstream http.url, exception events, and the gaps between siblings. Note that gateway proxy routes often produce a single-span trace; the deep JDBC/SQL chains show up on routes the gateway serves itself, such as /api/v1/permissions/me.

panels.title: LOGS FOR THE SELECTED TRACE
panels.description:
Simple: Every log message the app printed while handling that one specific request.

LOKI / LogQL. Loki's OTLP endpoint promotes service.name and the k8s.* resource attributes to labels; the log record's trace_id lands in structured metadata, which is what the `| trace_id=` filter matches. Requires -Dotel.logs.exporter=otlp on the app (you have it) — note the Instrumentation CR sets OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none, and the -D system property is what overrides it.

panels.title: FAILED REQUESTS — traces with errors or 5xx
panels.description:
Simple: Only the requests that failed or returned a server error, ready to click into.

TEMPO / TraceQL. Root-cause list for the ERROR INVESTIGATION workflow. Click through to the waterfall the same way.

targets.query: { resource.service.name = "$service_name" && kind = server && (status = error || span.http.response.status_code >= 500) } | select(span.http.request.method, span.http.route, span.http.response.status_code, resource.k8s.pod.name)

panels.title: SLOWEST JDBC / SQL SPANS
panels.description:
Simple: The slowest database queries across recent requests, with the actual SQL involved.

TEMPO / TraceQL. Prometheus only exposes HikariCP pool metrics (create / wait / use time) — it has no per-statement SQL latency. This panel is the per-statement view: it selects db spans directly out of Tempo, so you can see which SELECT is slow and jump to the whole request that issued it.

targets.query: { resource.service.name = "$service_name" && span.db.system != nil && duration >= $min_duration } | select(span.db.system, span.db.name, span.db.operation, span.db.sql.table, span.db.statement)

links.title: ▶ Load the full request that ran this SQL

value.title: ▶ Load the full request that ran this SQL

panels.title: Trace list (fallback — guaranteed-clickable trace IDs)
panels.description:
Simple: A simpler backup list of recent requests, in case the main table above has trouble loading.

Same TraceQL filter as the panel above but rendered with tableType = traces, whose trace-id column is always named `traceID`. Keep whichever of the two tables clicks through correctly in your Grafana build and delete the other.

targets.query: { resource.service.name = "$service_name" && kind = server && span.http.route =~ "$http_operation" && span.http.request.method =~ "$http_method" && duration >= $min_duration }

panels.title: HTTP status distribution
panels.description: Simple: What share of all requests fall into each response status code.

panels.title: Top failing endpoints (4xx / 5xx)

links.title: Open this endpoint's traces in Explore (Tempo)

panels.description: Simple: Which specific endpoints are producing the most errors right now.

panels.title: Application logs
panels.description:
Simple: Raw log messages from the app, filtered to warnings and errors by default.

LOKI / LogQL. Verified label set on your Loki: service_name, k8s_namespace_name, k8s_pod_name, k8s_deployment_name, k8s_container_name, deployment_environment, service_instance_id - plus detected_level, which Loki 3.x derives per line. Switch the 'Log level' variable to 'all levels' to see everything.

panels.title: Service dependency map
panels.description:
Simple: A visual map of what calls this service and what this service calls, with health shown at each connection.

PROMETHEUS / PromQL over Tempo metrics-generator series (traces_service_graph_*). Dependency overview only — it has no endpoint dimension. Use the trace waterfall for endpoint-level and request-level investigation.

panels.title: Outbound HTTP — request rate
panels.description: Simple: How often this service calls each external or downstream address.

panels.title: Outbound HTTP — P50 / P95 / P99
panels.description: Simple: How fast each downstream call responds, at typical and slow-case speeds.

panels.title: Outbound HTTP — 5xx %
panels.description:
Simple: What percent of calls to each downstream address are failing.

Per-destination denominator so a busy destination cannot mask a failing one. Destinations with no 5xx plot a real 0 rather than dropping out of the result - an empty ratio panel is indistinguishable from a broken one.

targets.expr: 100 * (sum by (server_address, http_request_method) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) or sum by (server_address, http_request_method) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace"}[$__rate_interval])) * 0) / sum by (server_address, http_request_method) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name=~"$service_name",deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment",k8s_namespace_name=~"$service_namespace"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Outbound dependencies — summary
panels.description: Simple: One table summarizing call volume, speed, and failures for every downstream address.

panels.title: Connection pool — used vs idle
panels.description:
Simple: How many database connections are actively in use versus sitting free.

db_client_connections_usage{state="used|idle"} plus db_client_connections_max. v9 queried db_client_operation_duration_seconds_*, which the OTel Java agent does not emit for JDBC — that is why the DB panels were empty.

panels.title: Connection pool saturation
panels.description: Simple: How close the database connection pool is to running out of free connections.

panels.title: Pending connection requests
panels.description:
Simple: Requests currently waiting in line for a free database connection — should normally be zero.

Anything above zero on 'pending' means threads are blocked waiting for a JDBC connection — the classic cause of a fast SQL query inside a slow HTTP request. NOTE: db_client_connections_timeouts_total is not emitted by your OTel Java agent build (verified against the Prometheus label API on 2026-08-11), so there is no pool-timeout series to chart; a sustained pending count is the signal to watch instead.

panels.title: Connection WAIT time (P50 / P95 / P99)
panels.description: Simple: How long requests wait to get a database connection before they can even start work.

panels.title: Connection USE time (P95 / P99)
panels.description:
Simple: How long a database connection is held once a request has one.

How long a borrowed connection is held — the closest Prometheus-side proxy for query duration. Per-statement SQL timing lives in the Tempo JDBC spans panel above.

panels.title: Connection CREATE time + borrow rate
panels.description:
Simple: How long it takes to open a brand-new database connection, and how often the app has to ask for one.

A rising create time or a high borrow rate with a saturated pool points at pool sizing rather than at the query.

panels.title: JVM CPU
panels.description:
Simple: How much CPU the application process itself is using.

v9 queried jvm_cpu_utilization_ratio, which does not exist. The OTel Java agent emits jvm.cpu.recent_utilization -> jvm_cpu_recent_utilization_ratio. Series B derives the same number from jvm_cpu_time_seconds_total / jvm_cpu_count as a fallback for older agent versions.

panels.title: JVM heap — used / committed / max
panels.description: Simple: How much of the app's memory (heap) is actually in use right now, versus its ceiling.

panels.title: JVM heap utilisation (% of max)
panels.description:
Simple: Memory usage as a percentage of the app's max allowed heap — climbing toward 100% is a warning sign.

Percent of jvm_memory_limit_bytes (true -Xmx), not of committed. v9 divided by committed, which understates pressure because committed grows with usage.

panels.title: JVM non-heap + memory by pool
panels.description: Simple: Memory the app uses outside the regular heap (like loaded class metadata), broken down by type.

panels.title: GC — time per second & pause P99
panels.description: Simple: How much time the app spends pausing to clean up unused memory (garbage collection), and how long the worst pauses are.

panels.title: GC — collections per second
panels.description: Simple: How often garbage collection is running — frequent runs can mean memory pressure.

panels.title: JVM threads — live / by state / peak
panels.description:
Simple: How many worker threads the app has running, and whether they're busy, waiting, or idle.

OTel's JVM instrumentation does not emit a peak-threads gauge (that is a Micrometer metric). 'peak (observed)' below is max_over_time() across the selected range, which is the honest equivalent from OTel data.

panels.title: JVM threads — daemon vs application
panels.description: Simple: Background (daemon) threads versus the app's own request-handling threads.

panels.title: Classes loaded / unloaded
panels.description: Simple: How many Java classes are currently loaded into memory — a steadily climbing number can indicate a class-loading leak.

panels.title: Replicas ready / desired
panels.description: Simple: How many copies of the app are supposed to be running versus how many actually are.

panels.title: Restarts (range)
panels.description: Simple: How many times the app's container has restarted in the selected time window.

panels.title: Pods not Ready
panels.description: Simple: How many copies of the app are currently unable to serve traffic.

panels.title: OOMKilled containers
panels.description: Simple: How many times the app was killed for using more memory than it was allowed.

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description:
Simple: Whether Kubernetes is holding back the app's CPU because it hit its limit.

REQUIRES RESOURCE LIMITS. Verified 2026-08-11: the api-gateway-backend-dev container declares `resources: {}` - no requests, no limits. kube_pod_container_resource_limits therefore emits nothing, and with no CPU quota the kernel never populates the CFS throttling counters. Set requests/limits on the Deployment and this panel fills in by itself.

panels.title: Pod phase
panels.description: Simple: The app container's current lifecycle state (e.g. Running).

panels.title: Pod CPU vs request / limit
panels.description:
Simple: Actual CPU usage compared to what was requested and the hard ceiling allowed.

Scoped to $k8s_workload — v9 showed every pod in the namespace because the Pod variable defaulted to All with no workload filter.

The usage series works; the dashed limit/request reference lines stay absent until the Deployment declares resources. REQUIRES RESOURCE LIMITS. Verified 2026-08-11: the api-gateway-backend-dev container declares `resources: {}` - no requests, no limits. kube_pod_container_resource_limits therefore emits nothing, and with no CPU quota the kernel never populates the CFS throttling counters. Set requests/limits on the Deployment and this panel fills in by itself.

panels.title: Pod memory vs limit
panels.description:
Simple: Actual memory usage compared to the hard ceiling — getting close risks the app being killed.

The usage series works; the dashed limit/request reference lines stay absent until the Deployment declares resources. REQUIRES RESOURCE LIMITS. Verified 2026-08-11: the api-gateway-backend-dev container declares `resources: {}` - no requests, no limits. kube_pod_container_resource_limits therefore emits nothing, and with no CPU quota the kernel never populates the CFS throttling counters. Set requests/limits on the Deployment and this panel fills in by itself.

panels.title: Memory utilisation (% of limit)
panels.description:
Simple: Memory usage as a percentage of the app's allowed limit.

REQUIRES RESOURCE LIMITS. Verified 2026-08-11: the api-gateway-backend-dev container declares `resources: {}` - no requests, no limits. kube_pod_container_resource_limits therefore emits nothing, and with no CPU quota the kernel never populates the CFS throttling counters. Set requests/limits on the Deployment and this panel fills in by itself.

panels.title: CPU throttling over time
panels.description:
Simple: How often, and by how much, the app's CPU has been throttled over time.

REQUIRES RESOURCE LIMITS. Verified 2026-08-11: the api-gateway-backend-dev container declares `resources: {}` - no requests, no limits. kube_pod_container_resource_limits therefore emits nothing, and with no CPU quota the kernel never populates the CFS throttling counters. Set requests/limits on the Deployment and this panel fills in by itself.

panels.title: Pod network RX / TX
panels.description: Simple: How much data the app is sending and receiving over the network.

panels.title: Container restarts & readiness
panels.description: Simple: Restart count and pass/fail readiness checks over time, side by side.

panels.title: Node CPU utilisation
panels.description: Simple: How busy the physical/virtual server (node) itself is, CPU-wise.

panels.title: Node memory utilisation
panels.description: Simple: How much memory the server itself has used, independent of any one app.

panels.title: Node load (1m / 5m / 15m per core)
panels.description: Simple: How many processes are waiting for CPU time on the server, averaged over 1/5/15 minutes.

panels.title: Node filesystem utilisation
panels.description: Simple: How full the server's disk is.

panels.title: Node disk I/O
panels.description: Simple: How much read/write activity is happening on the server's disk.

panels.title: Node network RX / TX
panels.description: Simple: Total network traffic in and out of the server.

panels.title: Pod density (running / allocatable)
panels.description: Simple: How many pods are running on the node versus how many it can hold.

panels.title: Node conditions
panels.description: Simple: Kubernetes' own health flags for the node (e.g. Ready, memory pressure, disk pressure).

panels.title: TELEMETRY PIPELINE HEALTH — check here first when panels say 'No data'
Collector — metric points sent vs FAILED, by exporter
panels.description:
Simple: How much telemetry data is making it out of the pipeline successfully versus being rejected.

Non-zero 'failed' on otlphttp/prometheus is the definitive proof that application metrics are not reaching Prometheus. The most common cause on this stack is out-of-order sample rejection by the Prometheus OTLP write receiver.

panels.title: Prometheus OTLP write endpoint — responses by code
panels.description:
Simple: Whether Prometheus is accepting or rejecting the metrics being pushed to it.

handler="/api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics". Any code other than 200/204 means Prometheus is rejecting the collector's metric writes.

panels.title: Collector — spans & logs sent vs FAILED
panels.description: Simple: Same success/failure check as above, but for traces and logs instead of metrics.

panels.title: Collector — export queue & memory-limiter drops
panels.description: Simple: Whether the pipeline is backed up or dropping data because it's overloaded.

panels.title: SANITY CHECK — what identity labels actually exist on the HTTP metric (ignores all dashboard filters)
panels.description:
Simple: Shows the real label names on the raw metric, ignoring every filter — use this to catch a label-name mismatch.

Deliberately unfiltered. If this table has rows but the panels above say 'No data', a dashboard VARIABLE is empty or wrong — compare the values here against the filter bar. If this table is empty too, the metric itself is not in Prometheus and the problem is the ingest pipeline, not the dashboard. 'Sample age' is seconds since that series was last written.

targets.expr: time() - max by (service_name, k8s_namespace_name, deployment_environment, job) (max_over_time(timestamp(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count)[$__range:1m]))

panels.title: Exporter Up
panels.description: 1 = connected, 0 = failed.

panels.title: Rollback Ratio %
panels.description: High values indicate application errors.

panels.title: Cache Hit Ratio %
panels.description: Target: >99% for OLTP workloads.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (database, datname) (rate(pg_stat_database_blks_hit{datname!="",database=~"$pg_database",datname=~"$pg_datname"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (database, datname) (rate(pg_stat_database_blks_hit{datname!="",database=~"$pg_database",datname=~"$pg_datname"}[5m]) + rate(pg_stat_database_blks_read{datname!="",database=~"$pg_database",datname=~"$pg_datname"}[5m])), 1)

panels.title: Rows Returned vs Fetched (Rate)
panels.description: Big gap = inefficient queries / missing indexes.

panels.title: Deadlocks (Rate)
panels.description: Any value above 0 needs investigation.

panels.title: Temp Files Created (Rate)
panels.description: High values = increase work_mem or optimize queries.

panels.title: Checkpoints â€” Timed vs Requested
panels.description: High 'requested' = increase max_wal_size.

panels.title: BGWriter â€” Buffers Written
panels.description: Backend direct writes (red) should be minimal.

panels.title: Table Seq Scan vs Index Scan
panels.description: A healthy system should favor index scans.

panels.title: Conflicts (Rate)
panels.description: Queries cancelled due to recovery conflict on standby replicas.

options.content:
### The investigation path

| Step | Panel | Datasource | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Golden Signals | Prometheus / PromQL | Is the service healthy at all? |
| 2 | API Endpoint Performance | Prometheus / PromQL | Which endpoint is slow or failing? |
| 3 | *click the row* | — | Sets `API Route` + `Method`, filtering everything below |
| 4 | Selected endpoint panels | Prometheus / PromQL | Is it all requests or a tail? Is the latency bi-modal? |
| 5 | API Requests | Tempo / TraceQL | Which individual requests were slow? |
| 6 | *click the row* | — | Sets `Selected Trace ID` |
| 7 | Selected trace waterfall | Tempo / TraceQL | Exactly where did the 89 ms go — controller, repository, Hikari `getConnection`, the SELECT, or a downstream call? |
| 8 | Logs for the selected trace | Loki / LogQL | What did the app actually log for that request? |
| 9 | JDBC pool / JVM / Pod / Node rows | Prometheus / PromQL | Was the cause the pool, the heap, throttling, or the node? |

### Grafana limitation, stated plainly
A Grafana table **cannot** expand a trace waterfall inside its own panel. The supported pattern — and the one used here — is: table row → data link → dashboard URL carrying `var-traceID` → a separate `traces` panel that queries Tempo by that ID. The redraw happens in this same browser tab, so it still behaves like a single window, but it is a variable round-trip, not an in-place expansion.

### Scope notes
* The **service dependency map** comes from Tempo's metrics-generator (`traces_service_graph_*`) and has no endpoint dimension by design. Use the waterfall for endpoint-level and request-level work.
* **Per-statement SQL latency is not in Prometheus.** The OTel Java agent emits HikariCP pool metrics only. Statement timing comes from the Tempo JDBC/SQL spans panel.
* **Peak threads** is a Micrometer metric, not an OTel one. The JVM threads panel shows `max_over_time()` across the selected range instead.
